section_summary: This section documents growing U.S. and Allied concern over exports to Japan of petroleum products, scrap iron, steel, bearings, aircraft-related goods, and strategic minerals such as copper, tungsten, tin, antimony, cobalt, and molybdenum. It includes public and congressional protests, State Department explanations of export controls, reports on Japanese purchasing in China and South America, and successful diplomatic efforts to prevent Dominican scrap-iron shipments. A substantial group of duplicated enclosures discusses Mauricio Hochschild’s mineral sales, followed by a La Paz despatch disputing his account of tungsten transactions involving Japan and Germany.

subfiles.title: L. R. Johnson letter forwarding a clipping about tank plate for Japan
subfiles.about: Johnson forwards a seemingly authentic report of tank-plate exports to Japan and calls it an inconsistency in American policy.
subfiles.summary: Johnson describes the enclosed item as sensational but apparently authentic. He suggests that the senator retain it for his files and expresses pleasure at the senator’s improving health.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Senator Bone on exports of tank plate
subfiles.about: The Department answers Senator Bone’s inquiry about tank-plate exports to Japan by supplying export-control regulations and policy statements.
subfiles.summary: Hull acknowledges Bone’s February 11 letter and the enclosed January 22 letter from L. R. Johnson. He supplies regulations, press releases, and a proclamation issued under the Export Control Act, emphasizing that licenses outside the British Empire and Western Hemisphere depend on national-defense needs. Johnson’s letter is returned.

subfiles.title: Fragment of London telegram no. 536 on British oil and raw-material exports
subfiles.about: The telegram reports British statements on oil supplies to Japan and export controls throughout the British Empire.
subfiles.summary: The surviving portion explains existing oil contracts with Japan and notes that most petroleum purchases from the United States faced no British legal obstacle apart from controls on aviation grades. Lord Cecil says exports from Britain, the colonies, and Dominions were licensed and that nickel and copper were sometimes completely barred outside the Empire and the United States. He stresses continuing consultation among British and Dominion governments.

subfiles.title: Tientsin telegram on large Japanese gasoline inquiries
subfiles.about: Caldwell reports Japanese inquiries for unusually large gasoline supplies for North China.
subfiles.summary: Standard Vacuum Oil Company had been asked through Mitsui Bussan for a quotation on 5.6 million gallons of gasoline, purportedly for the North China Communications Company. The firm offered only normal requirements through April, while an unconfirmed Mitsubishi order reportedly involved another 18.5 million gallons in drums. The buying effort was attributed to fears of frozen Japanese credits and a total gasoline embargo.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Hercules Powder Company pine-oil sales to Japan
subfiles.about: Yost records David Houston’s warning about rapidly increasing Japanese purchases of scarce American pine oil.
subfiles.summary: Japan’s purchases rose from a normal 70,000 gallons annually to roughly 330,000 gallons in 1940, and Japanese firms were requesting still larger monthly quantities. Pine oil was important as a flotation reagent for copper, zinc, and lead ores and therefore had potential military significance. Houston warned that restricting it could redirect Japanese demand toward cresylic acid, chiefly produced by Shell Oil.

subfiles.title: Representative Ford letter transmitting a petroleum-coke complaint
subfiles.about: Ford forwards William R. Harriman’s letter and a Los Angeles Times clipping concerning petroleum-coke sales to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Ford asks the State Department to consider the newspaper article and Harriman’s concern about petroleum-coke shipments. The letter formally transmits both items as enclosures.

subfiles.title: William R. Harriman letter on a petroleum-coke clipping
subfiles.about: Harriman sends Ford a Los Angeles Times clipping about petroleum-coke sales to Japan and suggests possible action.
subfiles.summary: Harriman notes that later legislation or regulation may already have addressed the issue. He nevertheless believes the October 27, 1940 article is worth Ford’s attention and perhaps congressional action.

subfiles.title: Hull reply to Representative Ford on petroleum-coke exports
subfiles.about: Hull says petroleum-coke exports and related issues are under interagency consideration.
subfiles.summary: Hull thanks Ford for forwarding Harriman’s letter and the Los Angeles Times clipping. He states that the Department and other government agencies are considering petroleum coke and related products with a view to whatever action may prove appropriate. Harriman’s letter is returned.

subfiles.title: Senator Wiley letter enclosing an Auburn clipping on suspicious shipments
subfiles.about: Wiley sends Hull a newspaper item alleging suspicious westbound shipments of TNT, rails, and tank plate.
subfiles.summary: The enclosed Auburn Globe-Republican article describes TNT addressed to a Pacific shipping company and other rail and tank-plate shipments believed destined overseas. It claims that similar traffic frequently passed through Auburn. Wiley offers the item for Hull’s consideration.

subfiles.title: State Department reply on licensing controlled exports
subfiles.about: Hull explains the Department’s licensing policy for strategic exports in response to the suspicious-shipment clipping.
subfiles.summary: Licenses were generally issued to the British Empire and Western Hemisphere when American surpluses allowed. Aviation gasoline and scrap iron were prohibited outside those areas, while other controlled goods were licensed sparingly. Hull emphasizes that controls were continually adjusted to national-defense requirements.

subfiles.title: Representative Hendricks letter forwarding a constituent appeal
subfiles.about: Hendricks forwards a Florida correspondent’s letter and resolution concerning exports and asks for consideration.
subfiles.summary: The OCR obscures much of the constituent’s identity and the wording of the appeal. The surviving text shows that Hendricks respectfully transmitted the communication and its accompanying resolution to the Secretary of State.

subfiles.title: Hull reply to Representative Hendricks regarding further restrictions
subfiles.about: Hull states that additional export restrictions are under continuing interagency consideration and returns the constituent materials.
subfiles.summary: The surviving portion says that the question of further restrictions was receiving constant and careful consideration by all interested government agencies. Miss Barto’s letter and enclosure were returned. The listed informational enclosures included the National Defense Act, proclamations, executive materials, and a resolution.

subfiles.title: Ciudad Trujillo telegram reporting scrap iron intended for Japan
subfiles.from: G. Howland Shaw Scotten, Ciudad Trujillo
subfiles.about: Scotten asks whether he should approach the Dominican government about 1,000 tons of scrap iron reportedly awaiting shipment to Japan.
subfiles.summary: A Japanese steamer was expected around March 6 to collect approximately 1,000 tons of scrap iron from the Ciudad Trujillo wharf. In light of U.S. policy, Scotten requested instructions on making an official or informal approach to Dominican authorities.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on the Dominican prohibition of scrap-iron exports
subfiles.about: The memorandum reports that Dominican customs had barred scrap-iron exports without prior Treasury authorization.
subfiles.summary: The action followed exchanges between the American Legation and the Department concerning a proposed shipment to Japan. A February 25 circular from the Deputy Receiver of Dominican Customs ordered customs offices not to permit scrap-iron exports without Treasury approval.

subfiles.title: Dominican customs circular prohibiting unauthorized scrap-iron exports
subfiles.about: The circular orders Dominican customs offices to prevent scrap-iron exports unless previously authorized by the Treasury and Commerce Secretariat.
subfiles.summary: Circular Letter No. 463 implements an instruction from the Dominican Secretariat of the Treasury and Commerce. It requires all customs personnel to comply with the prohibition on unauthorized exports of old iron.

subfiles.title: Instruction to Ciudad Trujillo concerning Cuban general export licenses
subfiles.about: The instruction transmits information about U.S. general export licenses for Cuba and rules governing reexports.
subfiles.summary: Specified controlled articles could be exported to Cuba under general licenses, while other controlled goods still required individual licenses. The Department was considering comparable general licenses for additional Western Hemisphere countries. The first page is heavily corrupted by OCR.

subfiles.title: Telegram directing an informal approach to the Dominican government
subfiles.about: Hull instructs the Legation to seek Dominican cooperation in preventing scrap-iron exports outside the Western Hemisphere.
subfiles.summary: The Legation was to explain confidentially that the United States, Colombia, Cuba, Mexico, and other countries had restricted exports of scrap iron and other defense materials outside the hemisphere. Hull expressed hope that the Dominican government would adopt the same policy. He also noted strong American domestic demand for scrap iron.

subfiles.title: Under Secretary’s note recommending a Dominican approach
subfiles.about: Welles recommends a confidential explanation of U.S. scrap-iron policy to the Dominican government.
subfiles.summary: Bonsal was asked to consult Maxwell Hamilton. Unless Hamilton objected, Welles favored informing the Dominican government of the U.S. position and Mexico’s precedent, while expressing hope for matching Dominican cooperation.

subfiles.title: New Sing appeal for stronger restrictions on Japan
subfiles.about: Sing urges the United States to stop supplying Japan with war materials and asks why stronger action has not been taken.
subfiles.summary: Writing for Chinese students in Mississippi, Sing argues that Chinese resistance remained vital to American security. He asks whether Japan was still purchasing large quantities of basic war materials, why public support for an embargo had not produced further action, and why the United States continued supplying a new Axis member.

subfiles.title: Hamilton reply to New Sing on export controls
subfiles.about: Hamilton acknowledges Sing’s appeal and supplies laws and regulations governing exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton says the Department carefully noted both the letter and the spirit behind it. He encloses the National Defense Act, proclamations, regulations, and White House releases explaining the export-licensing system. Aviation gasoline, lubricating oil, and iron and steel scrap were specifically restricted, while other commodities were subject to varying controls based on U.S. defense needs.

subfiles.title: Commerce Department inquiry about discarded rails
subfiles.about: Wythe requests specifications and location information needed to assess possible American interest in discarded rails.
subfiles.summary: The Metals and Minerals Division had consulted the Iron and Steel Scrap Institute. The institute expected interest but doubted the opportunity justified a special trip without details on the rails’ condition, attachments, weight, inland location, and distance from port.

subfiles.title: British Embassy letter on a cobalt shipment aboard SS Imperial
subfiles.about: Dent reports Chilean action that may prevent a cobalt shipment to Japan aboard the SS Imperial.
subfiles.summary: The Caja de Crédito Minero refused the transaction and gave the correspondence to Chile’s foreign minister, stating that it had never dealt with the Overseas Metal and Ore Corporation. Dent welcomed the likely prevention of the Japanese shipment and promised further information about the cobalt’s loading point and origin. He also clarified that the cobalt was already aboard when the vessel reached New York and therefore required no U.S. export license.

subfiles.title: Telegram requesting investigation of 4,000 tons of Dominican scrap
subfiles.from: Sumner Welles, Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Welles asks the Legation to investigate a reported 4,000-ton scrap shipment to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Harry Harris and Company reported that Emeterio Sotomayor possessed scrap containing steel, cast iron, and 250 tons of nickel-steel armor plate. The material was allegedly about to be loaded aboard a Japanese ship. The Department stated that it would not welcome such a shipment.

subfiles.title: Scotten telegram promising Dominican cooperation
subfiles.from: G. Howland Shaw Scotten, Ciudad Trujillo
subfiles.about: Scotten reports that the Dominican president promised to prevent scrap-iron shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Scotten personally raised the issue with the president. The president assured him of complete cooperation in hemisphere defense and said the Dominican government would act immediately to stop scrap iron from going to Japan.

subfiles.title: John S. Taylor appeal to stop all aid to Japan
subfiles.about: Taylor urges Bryson to introduce legislation ending American exports and assistance to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Taylor calls it astonishing that the United States supplied Japan with scrap iron, gasoline, and other goods while aiding China. He argues that most Americans opposed the policy and encourages Bryson to sponsor an immediate comprehensive cutoff.

subfiles.title: Hull letter returning the Taylor correspondence to Bryson
subfiles.about: Hull acknowledges Bryson’s transmittal of Taylor’s protest and encloses a copy of the Department’s reply.
subfiles.summary: Hull identifies the subject as exports of materials to Japan. He returns Taylor’s February 21 letter and provides Bryson with a copy of the response sent directly to Taylor.

subfiles.title: Hochschild report on South American mineral exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Hochschild surveys Japanese purchases of strategic minerals from Chile, Bolivia, Peru, and Argentina and proposes measures to redirect the trade.
subfiles.summary: Japan bought Chilean copper and molybdenum, Bolivian copper, antimony, tin, and wolframite, Peruvian copper, molybdenum, wolframite, and lead, and Argentine tin-plate residues and tungsten. Hochschild attributes the trade to Japanese price advantages, textile countertrade, and the absence of coordinated restrictions. He argues that ending it would require South American governmental cooperation and long-term U.S. purchasing commitments at stable prices.

subfiles.title: Feis acknowledgment to Schubart concerning Hochschild’s report
subfiles.about: Feis thanks Schubart for the Hochschild report and circulates it within the Department.
subfiles.summary: Feis acknowledges receipt of Schubart’s note and the photostat of Hochschild’s letter on South American mineral sales to Japan. He says the communications are being brought to the attention of interested Department offices.

subfiles.title: Instruction forwarding the Hochschild papers to Santiago
subfiles.about: The Department sends the Schubart and Hochschild correspondence to the Embassy in Santiago for information.
subfiles.summary: The instruction identifies Schubart’s January 28 cover letter and Hochschild’s January 27 report. It highlights mineral and metal exports from Chile, Bolivia, Peru, and Argentina to Japan.

subfiles.title: Schubart cover letter concerning accusations against Hochschild
subfiles.about: Schubart forwards Hochschild’s explanation of his companies’ ore sales to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Schubart says Hochschild had been accused of unpatriotic tungsten sales but had offered explanations Schubart found satisfactory. He sends a photostatic copy so the government can assess the claims and adds that Hochschild had promised cooperation.

subfiles.title: Hochschild mineral-export report enclosed for Santiago
subfiles.about: This enclosure details mineral exports from four South American countries to Japan and recommends a coordinated purchasing alternative.
subfiles.summary: The report describes Japanese buying of copper, molybdenum, antimony, tin, wolframite, lead, and tin-plate residues. Hochschild emphasizes Japanese price premiums and trade in cheap textiles, while noting that British officials knew of the shipments. He proposes stable long-term U.S. purchases and governmental cooperation as the practical means of stopping the flow.

subfiles.title: Instruction forwarding the Hochschild papers to La Paz
subfiles.about: The Department sends the Schubart and Hochschild correspondence to the Legation in Bolivia.
subfiles.summary: The instruction encloses Schubart’s January 28 letter and Hochschild’s January 27 report. It calls attention to mineral and metal exports from Chile, Bolivia, Peru, and Argentina to Japan.

subfiles.title: Schubart cover letter enclosed for La Paz
subfiles.about: Schubart explains why he is providing Hochschild’s account of South American ore sales to Japan.
subfiles.summary: He recounts accusations that Hochschild’s tungsten sales were unpatriotic and says he had found Hochschild’s explanations satisfactory. Schubart invites government verification of the report and stresses Hochschild’s stated willingness to cooperate.

subfiles.title: Hochschild mineral-export report enclosed for La Paz
subfiles.about: The report surveys Japanese mineral procurement across South America, with particular attention to Bolivian wolframite.
subfiles.summary: Hochschild says small and medium Bolivian producers favored Japan’s higher tungsten prices and that the Banco Minero would handle the trade even if his firm withdrew. He offers similar accounts of Chilean, Peruvian, and Argentine exports. He recommends coordinated government action and guaranteed U.S. purchases to replace Japanese demand.

subfiles.title: Instruction forwarding the Hochschild papers to Lima
subfiles.about: The Department forwards the Schubart and Hochschild correspondence to the Embassy in Peru.
subfiles.summary: The instruction encloses the January 28 Schubart letter and January 27 Hochschild report. The subject is strategic mineral and metal exports from Chile, Bolivia, Peru, and Argentina to Japan.

subfiles.title: Schubart cover letter enclosed for Lima
subfiles.about: Schubart forwards Hochschild’s defense of his South American companies’ sales to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Schubart reports recurring allegations that Hochschild was unpatriotic because his firms sold tungsten to Japan. He regards Hochschild’s explanations as satisfactory but provides the letter for independent government checking. He also records Hochschild’s offer to cooperate.

subfiles.title: Hochschild mineral-export report enclosed for Lima
subfiles.about: The enclosure describes Japanese purchases of South American strategic minerals and suggests replacing them with stable American demand.
subfiles.summary: The report covers Chilean copper and molybdenum, Bolivian tungsten and other ores, Peruvian molybdenum, wolframite and lead, and Argentine tungsten. Japanese firms offered better prices and supported the trade through textile sales and return freight. Hochschild argues that an effective embargo required cooperation from the producing governments and long-term U.S. purchase contracts.

subfiles.title: Instruction forwarding the Hochschild papers to Buenos Aires
subfiles.about: The Department sends the Schubart and Hochschild correspondence to the Embassy in Argentina.
subfiles.summary: The instruction encloses Schubart’s cover letter and Hochschild’s report. It identifies exports of minerals and metals from Chile, Bolivia, Peru, and Argentina to Japan as the subject.

subfiles.title: Schubart cover letter enclosed for Buenos Aires
subfiles.about: Schubart submits Hochschild’s account of ore sales to Japan for government examination.
subfiles.summary: Schubart describes rumors accusing Hochschild of unpatriotic tungsten trading. He says Hochschild’s explanations had satisfied him, but he sends the report so officials can verify its accuracy. Hochschild was said to be willing to cooperate with the government.

subfiles.title: Hochschild mineral-export report enclosed for Buenos Aires
subfiles.about: The report describes Japanese mineral purchases in South America and proposes economic measures to curtail them.
subfiles.summary: Hochschild explains how Japanese prices and textile countertrade drew copper, tungsten, antimony, tin, molybdenum, and lead away from other markets. He says the producing governments followed the example of continuing U.S. exports to Japan and would need incentives to change course. His proposed solution combines diplomatic cooperation with fixed-price, long-term U.S. purchasing.

subfiles.title: Feis memorandum to Welles on the Hochschild communication
subfiles.about: Feis calls Welles’s attention to Hochschild’s letter amid discussions of South American strategic-material sales to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum says the Bank of Manhattan communication and Hochschild’s attached letter are pertinent to current policy discussions. Its focus is the sale of strategic and critical materials from South America to Japan.

subfiles.title: Immigration Section general-card-index search sheet
subfiles.from: Division of Communication and Records, Immigration Section
subfiles.about: The sheet records a search for file numbers under an alien’s name, but no usable name or entries appear in the OCR.
subfiles.summary: Only the printed form headings are legible. The page does not preserve an identifiable person’s name or any file-number results.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on alleged Mexican concessions to Japanese interests
subfiles.about: The memorandum flags a New York Times article about concessions allegedly granted by Mexican official Modesto C. Rolland.
subfiles.summary: The writer notes allegations that Rolland favored Japanese interests and also promised concessions to American promoters. One example involved an option for manganese sales associated with H. K. Kicklighter and a Mr. Allen. The surviving ending is incomplete.

subfiles.title: New York Times clipping, “Mexico Opens Inquiry”
subfiles.about: The clipping reports a Mexican investigation into alleged maladministration benefiting Japanese commercial interests.
subfiles.summary: Mexico’s attorney general opened the inquiry at the Senate’s request, focusing on actions by former under secretary Modesto C. Rolland. Rolland was linked to an oil concession for a Japanese-controlled company and to an import permit allegedly favorable to another Japanese concern. Much of the lower portion is obscured by OCR.

subfiles.title: Robinson letter on petroleum export-control definitions
subfiles.about: Robinson recommends wording and technical thresholds for controlling crude oils and aviation lubricants.
subfiles.summary: Robinson and Dr. Wilson reject “economically feasible commercial processes” as too dependent on personal interpretation and recommend returning to “commercial distillation.” They propose lowering the viscosity-index threshold to 65 so Pennsylvania and suitable Mid-Continent crudes would be controlled while Gulf Coast and California crudes remained exportable. Robinson also argues that the separate aviation-lubricant provision already covered steam-refined stocks.

subfiles.title: Senator Wiley letter concerning alleged Ford aircraft bombing Canton
subfiles.about: Wiley asks Hamilton to comment on a clergyman’s allegation that Ford-built aircraft had bombed Canton.
subfiles.summary: Wiley forwards Reverend Edwin O. Kennedy’s protest and requests a duplicate response. He also asks that the enclosure be returned for his files.

subfiles.title: Kennedy protest over alleged American-made bombers in Canton
subfiles.about: Kennedy protests reports that aircraft bearing Henry Ford’s name were used to bomb Canton.
subfiles.summary: Friends recently returned from China had told Kennedy they were bombed in Canton by planes marked with Ford’s name. He asks Wiley to prevent American participation in destruction in China through war-supply sales to Japan.

subfiles.title: Hull reply on aircraft exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Hull responds that no aircraft were exported to Japan in 1940 and only one in 1939 under U.S. export licenses.
subfiles.summary: Hull encloses a February 18 press release listing arms and war-supply exports during 1940. He adds that Ford had produced only a few planes in 1932 before discontinuing aircraft operations, making current bombing by Ford-built planes highly unlikely unless the aircraft were very old. Kennedy’s letter is returned.

subfiles.title: Timken renewed inquiry about bearing exports to Japan and Russia
subfiles.from: W. E. Umstattd, Timken Roller Bearing Company
subfiles.about: Timken seeks an unofficial policy judgment before fulfilling substantial Japanese bearing orders.
subfiles.summary: The company had $270,000 in Japanese orders scheduled for March through May and new inquiries worth $75,000 for machine-tool bearings. Citing increased Far Eastern tension, its president renews an earlier request for guidance on exports to Japan and Russia.

subfiles.title: Timken’s original inquiry on sales to Japan and Russia
subfiles.about: Timken asks whether continued acceptance of Japanese and Russian bearing orders accords with government policy.
subfiles.summary: Although bearing exports to both countries had historically been negligible, Japanese purchases were increasing as supplies shifted away from Germany and Sweden. The company understood formal embargoes but also perceived unofficial disapproval of some less directly military goods. It sought guidance because it did not wish to act contrary to government policy.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to O. J. Cannon on scrap-iron licenses
subfiles.about: The Department denies that scrap-iron export licenses were issued for Japan and asks Cannon to identify the ships he observed.
subfiles.summary: The reply states that iron and steel scrap could be licensed only for the Western Hemisphere and Great Britain, under the President’s September 26, 1940 policy. Cannon is asked to provide ship names and destinations for vessels he believed were loading scrap iron.

subfiles.title: La Paz despatch challenging Hochschild’s account of tungsten sales
subfiles.from: Allan Dawson, American Legation, La Paz
subfiles.about: Dawson disputes Hochschild’s claim that a British blockade expert encouraged continued tungsten sales to Japan.
subfiles.summary: J. L. Royden had reportedly sought to stop Japanese acquisition of Bolivian tungsten and antimony because the materials could reach Germany through Japanese intermediaries; a British Legation officer dismissed Hochschild’s contrary account as “poppycock.” Dawson reports allegations that Hochschild sold tungsten to the Banco Minero, which then exported it to Japan, obscuring the true scale of Hochschild-related sales. He nevertheless agrees that stable long-term U.S. purchase contracts could help divert Bolivian production from Japan.

subfiles.title: Singapore telegram on Malayan tin and rubber controls
subfiles.about: Patton reports that Malaya would maintain stringent limits on tin and rubber exports to Japan to prevent indirect supply to Germany.
subfiles.summary: The Japanese consul general had complained about the restricted export quotas. The colonial secretary replied that Japanese assurances against reexport to Germany would not suffice because Japan could consume Malayan supplies while reexporting equivalent imports from Thailand or Indochina. Increased Japanese purchases elsewhere would therefore be offset by further reductions in authorized Malayan exports.

subfiles.title: Congressional referral slip transmitting an enclosure to the State Department
subfiles.about: An unidentified congressional office refers an enclosed communication to the State Department for consideration and a report.
subfiles.summary: The form requests favorable consideration consistent with the merits of the enclosed communication. It also asks that a report accompany the return of the enclosure, but the underlying subject and sender are not legible.
